Forty meters of air, then the ocean. That is the drop from a cruise ship's top deck at twenty knots.
Around two dozen people go over the side of cruise ships every single year, and only one in five of them ever comes home alive.
The fall lasts under three seconds and you hit the water near ninety kilometers an hour, so go in feet first, arms crossed.
Then the real danger begins, because cold water forces an involuntary gasp, and if your face is under, that gasp is seawater.
Survival experts have a rule for this, and its first number is sixty seconds spent doing nothing but slowing your breath.
A hundred thousand tons at twenty knots cannot simply stop, it covers ten meters every second and needs a kilometer to halt.
If someone saw you fall, a lifebuoy trailing light and smoke marks your spot in the water while the captain loops the ship back.
That turn takes fifteen minutes, and the rule's second number, ten minutes, is how long your arms keep working in cold water.
Temperature decides everything, warm Caribbean water buys most of a day, ten degree water buys one hour.
Instinct says swim, but swimming drains heat far faster, so hug your knees to your chest and let the ring hold you.
Here is the twist, cruise railings stand over a meter tall by law, so nobody slips, people climb them for a photo.
So float, never swim, and remember this began on the wrong side of a railing, forty meters of air, one mistake.
